title: Seventy years of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh
author: Editorial Desk
summary: BMS completed seventy years on 23 July 2025. What the year of celebration included, what was said in Delhi, and the questions the anniversary raises.
body:
*Photo: BMS seventieth anniversary celebration, July 2025*

On **23 July 2025** the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh completed seventy years. The date matters to the organisation because it was on 23 July 1955, the birth anniversary of Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, that BMS was founded in Bhopal by Dattopant Thengadi. A year-long programme of celebrations, launched in Bhopal on 23 July 2024, ended with a concluding event in Delhi. BMS described the whole exercise as a time to look back, to introspect, and to ask what remains to be done. This post sets out what happened, what the numbers and claims are, and what the anniversary says about the road ahead.

## How the idea began

Accounts from within the organisation describe a labour movement that began small and was often not taken seriously. Thengadi, an RSS pracharak and a lawyer by training, had been organising workers from about 1949 and concluded that the labour organisations of the day used workers for political ends and did not serve labour, industry or the nation. BMS records that he presented his report at the first annual conference on 12 August 1967. An article in Organiser says the organisation's slogan of *industrialise the nation, labourise the industry and nationalise the labour* was at first dismissed as a joke.

Growth came slowly. Wikipedia notes that BMS's first national executive was elected in 1967, twelve years after founding. A Labour Ministry verification of union membership recorded 62,15,797 members for BMS in 2002 on provisional figures, while BMS itself claims more than a crore. BMS President Hiranmay Pandya said at the anniversary that BMS was the second-largest central union until 1981 and became the largest by 1989. These are claims by the organisation and, in the case of the earlier years, by BMS-aligned writers, and readers should treat them as the organisation's own account.

## The year of celebration

The programme was built around contact with workers and not only ceremony. According to an Organiser report ahead of the main event, it included:

- the launch of the celebration in Bhopal on 23 July 2024;
- a five-month series of district-level lectures on five themes, starting in August 2024;
- the *Shramik Sampark* outreach to workers, which ran from December; and
- district-level women's and youth conferences in the early months of 2025.

The five themes are worth noting. BMS has long spoken of the environment, social harmony and swadeshi, and Pandya said two more had been added: *kutumb prabodhan*, or strengthening the family, and *nagrik kartavya*, or civic duty. Together they show how BMS sees itself: as an organisation that speaks about wages but does not limit itself to them. Pandya said in an interview that BMS is not merely about pay, perks and promotion.

## The Delhi event of 23 July

The concluding programme was held at the KD Jadhav Wrestling Hall in Indira Gandhi Stadium, New Delhi. The chief guest was RSS Sarsanghchalak Dr Mohan Bhagwat, and the Union Labour and Employment Minister, Dr Mansukh Mandaviya, was guest of honour. The BMS website lists Ravindra Himte, the General Secretary, as giving an overview of the seventy-year journey, and Pandya as speaking and launching an app called E-Karyakarta, meant for records of karyakartas and for internal communication. A documentary on the seventy years was screened, senior activists were felicitated, and a special edition of Organiser Weekly titled *Laborious Resetting* was released. Pre-event reports expected around ten thousand karyakartas, with the proceedings streamed live to about 110 locations over Zoom and YouTube.

Some of what was said gives a picture of the occasion. Bhagwat described BMS as a values-based movement and said every generation must understand why it carries on the work. He spoke of the unorganised sector, the restoration of dignity for workers and technology. He said that technology cannot be rejected, but it should be used for the benefit of society, and that BMS should ensure that new developments help every section. Mandaviya, for his part, said the labour movement should drive nation-building and not just protest. Pandya announced **BMS@100** as the next milestone.

## What seventy years add up to

The organisation points to a number of things.

- **A national centre.** BMS describes itself as the largest central trade union organisation in India. A BMS-aligned article puts it in more than 620 districts, with over 6,500 affiliated unions in 44 industries, though that is the author's figure and not an independently audited one.
- **Federations in many sectors.** The BMS website lists nearly forty federations, from railways, banks, insurance, postal and telecom services to construction, mines, plantations, jute, ports, electricity and scheme workers such as Anganwadi, ASHA and mid-day meal employees.
- **A distinct philosophy.** It is summarised in three lines: *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*, meaning national interest, industry's interest and the worker's interest, and the slogan *Workers, unite the world*, which BMS offers in place of the older *Workers of the world, unite*.
- **A voice at international forums.** BMS has taken part in International Labour Conference sessions and the BRICS Trade Union Forum. It chaired the Labour 20 engagement group during India's G20 presidency in 2022-23, which Pandya said involved about 62 delegates from 29 countries. Mandaviya said BMS had led a 30-member Indian delegation to the ILO.

## Questions the anniversary raises

A milestone invites two questions: what was learnt, and what is next? BMS's own pointers for the future are the unorganised sector, which Organiser describes as about nine-tenths of the workforce, platform and gig workers, scheme workers, and the effect of new technology on jobs. These are also the areas where the law has been changing, since the four Labour Codes that came into force in November 2025 define gig and platform work in statute for the first time.

There are also questions that every long-established union faces: how to bring in younger members, how to ensure that women lead as well as join, and how to keep records that are accurate. Pandya spoke of young people and women leading and not only being represented, and the E-Karyakarta app is an attempt at the records problem. Whether these efforts succeed will be visible in the next membership verification.

## An old principle

Bhagwat recalled advice that Golwalkar had given to Thengadi: durable labour work has to rest on genuine care for the worker. Thengadi himself is remembered for the idea that an organisation grows by the quality of its karyakartas. That may be the best test of the seventy years, and of the thirty that BMS has set as its next target.
